desc:
Choose a set of positions in s and a set of positions in t (either set may be empty). The two choices form a matching pair if the characters picked from s, read left to right, spell exactly the same string as the characters picked from t.

Count the matching pairs of position sets. Two pairs are different when their position sets differ, even if they spell the same text, and the pair of two empty sets counts. Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

s = "ab",  t = "ab"  ->  4   (empty/empty, a/a, b/b, ab/ab)
s = "aa",  t = "a"   ->  3   (empty/empty, s[0]/t[0], s[1]/t[0])
s = "abc", t = "xyz"  ->  1   (only empty/empty)
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Count prefixes first: let f(i, j) be the number of matching pairs that use only the first i characters of s and the first j characters of t. What is f(0, j)?

Split the pairs counted by f(i, j) by whether s[i] is used and whether t[j] is used. The pairs where s[i] is unused number f(i-1, j), those where t[j] is unused number f(i, j-1), and those where neither is used are counted twice.

Pairs that use both s[i] and t[j] as their last characters exist only if s[i] == t[j], and there are exactly f(i-1, j-1) of them. So f(i, j) = f(i-1, j) + f(i, j-1) - f(i-1, j-1) + (f(i-1, j-1) if s[i] == t[j]).
editorial: Let f(i, j) count matching pairs inside the prefixes s[:i] and t[:j]. When one prefix is empty the only possible pair is the empty one, so f(0, j) = f(i, 0) = 1.

For i, j ≥ 1 split by the last characters. Pairs that do not use s[i-1] are counted by f(i-1, j); pairs that do not use t[j-1] by f(i, j-1); pairs that use neither are in both, and there are f(i-1, j-1) of them, so inclusion-exclusion removes them once. What remains are pairs that use both last characters. For such a pair, both position sets end in the last character, so the two last characters must be equal, and what is left is any matching pair of the shorter prefixes: f(i-1, j-1) choices. This term is added only if s[i-1] == t[j-1].

Note that this counts pairs of position sets, unlike the count of distinct common strings, which needs a different technique. Apply the modulus at each cell (subtracting can go negative, so reduce with % MOD after adding). Two rolling rows give O(n) memory.
solution:
def countCommonSubsequencePairs(s, t):
    MOD = 10 ** 9 + 7
    n = len(t)
    prev = [1] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, len(s) + 1):
        cur = [1] * (n + 1)
        c = s[i - 1]
        for j in range(1, n + 1):
            v = prev[j] + cur[j - 1] - prev[j - 1]
            if c == t[j - 1]:
                v += prev[j - 1]
            cur[j] = v % MOD
        prev = cur
    return prev[n]
